argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0202c: meeting "c" (conceptual design) of series SY0202.

PROJECT
The team is designing a library self-checkout kiosk.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  Industrial Designer (ID)  Tomas  present
B  Marketing Expert (ME)  Priya  present
C  User Interface designer (UI)  Hannah  present
D  Project Manager (PM)  Marcus  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0202a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting, the team introduced themselves, and he presented the project: a self-checkout kiosk for public library networks. He gave the budget targets from the brief: a production cost under 4,000 euros per unit and a selling price of around 6,500 euros. The brief also asks that the kiosk fit the look of a library rather than resemble a cash machine. The team agreed that the kiosk will handle checkout and renewals but not returns. They also agreed that borrowers will identify themselves with either a library card or a library-app digital card, both read by the same scanner. The team discussed barcode versus RFID book reading, an email-only receipt, and a touchscreen-only interface, but did not settle any of these. The marketing expert raised accessibility as a key requirement and took on researching it. The project manager then assigned individual preparation tasks for the functional design meeting.
  decisions: The kiosk will support checkout and renewals only; returns stay with the existing book drop. Borrowers will identify themselves with a library card or a library-app digital card (QR code), both read by one scanner. The production cost target stays fixed at under 4,000 euros per unit.
  actions: The industrial designer will work out the working design: the internal components and a rough layout. The user interface designer will prepare the technical functions design: the step-by-step checkout and renewal flow and the screens. The marketing expert will prepare the user requirements, drawing on her meeting with library services staff. The marketing expert will gather the accessibility requirements from library services and share them with the user interface designer. The user interface designer had first offered to do this. The project manager will send round the project brief and the notes from the meeting. Someone should check the cost of RFID readers, but no one took this task.
  problems: It is unclear whether the kiosk should read barcodes, RFID tags or both. The cost of RFID readers is unknown, and no one is assigned to check it. The team did not decide whether to drop the printed receipt in favour of email or to make printing optional. The team did not decide whether the interface should be touchscreen-only or include at least one hardware button such as cancel or help.
  action item SY0202a.ai1: Prepare the working design: internal components and a rough layout of the kiosk (owner A, active)
  action item SY0202a.ai2: Prepare the technical functions design: step-by-step checkout and renewal flow and screens (owner C, active)
  action item SY0202a.ai3: Prepare user requirements from libraries and borrowers (owner B, active)
  action item SY0202a.ai4: Gather accessibility requirements (wheelchair height, screen readers) from library services and share them with the UI designer (owner B, active)
  action item SY0202a.ai5: Check what RFID readers cost (owner no owner, active)
  action item SY0202a.ai6: Send round the project brief and the meeting notes (owner D, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer proposed supporting both barcode and RFID reading; this was not decided because of the RFID cost.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer proposed dropping the printed receipt in favour of email; the marketing expert objected and the decision was postponed.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer proposed an all-touchscreen interface with no physical buttons; the industrial designer wanted at least one hardware button, and the question was left for the next meeting.

[SY0202b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting, noted that the user interface designer was absent through illness, and confirmed that he had sent round the brief and the kickoff notes. He recapped the earlier decisions: checkout and renewals only, and one scanner for library cards and app QR codes. The industrial designer presented the working design: an embedded PC, a fifteen-inch touchscreen, a card and QR scanner, a barcode or RFID book reader, and a small thermal printer. Without RFID, his rough cost estimate came to about 2,900 euros, and the wood-panelled casing was the largest cost. The marketing expert presented the user requirements and the accessibility requirements from library services. These covered speed, the fact that about a third of borrowers want printed slips, wheelchair reach heights, audio output, and a physical button. The team agreed on email receipts by default with optional printing, and on one hardware help button with everything else on the touchscreen. They also agreed to lower the book shelf to accessible heights. The RFID pricing task was first given to the industrial designer and then passed to the marketing expert, because library services already has an RFID supplier price list. The barcode versus RFID decision was left open until those numbers are available.
  decisions: Receipts will be sent by email by default, and borrowers can choose to print one; the printer stays in the design. The kiosk will have one physical help button. The button calls staff, and holding it switches on audio mode. All other controls stay on the touchscreen. The layout will follow the accessibility heights: the book shelf will be about 75 to 80 cm instead of 90 cm, and no controls will be above about 120 cm. The kiosk will provide audio support, with a headphone jack and spoken instructions, for visually impaired borrowers.
  actions: The marketing expert will get RFID reader and tag prices from library services' existing supplier. This task was first assigned to the industrial designer. The user interface designer, who was absent, will update the checkout and renewal flow for the help button, audio mode and print option, and will send round her draft screens before the next meeting. The marketing expert will email the accessibility requirements to the user interface designer today. The industrial designer will prepare sketches of the casing look and materials, using the new accessible heights. The project manager will write up and circulate the notes and brief the user interface designer on the button decision.
  problems: The choice between barcode and RFID, or supporting both, is still open until the RFID prices are known. It is unclear whether adding RFID keeps the unit under the 4,000-euro production cost target. Some library branches may still be barcode-only and not RFID-tagged. The user interface designer has not yet presented the flow or screens, and she was absent when the hardware button was decided against her earlier all-touchscreen proposal.
  action item SY0202b.ai1: Check the cost of RFID readers and tags, using library services' existing supplier price list. This follows up the unowned SY0202a.ai5. (owner B, reassigned)
  action item SY0202b.ai2: Update the checkout and renewal flow for the hardware help button, audio mode and optional print, and send round the draft screens before the next meeting (owner C, active)
  action item SY0202b.ai3: Email the accessibility requirements from library services to the user interface designer. This carries over SY0202a.ai4. (owner B, active)
  action item SY0202b.ai4: Prepare sketches of the casing look and materials (wood panelling), using the new accessible heights (owner A, active)
  action item SY0202b.ai5: Write up and circulate the meeting notes and brief the user interface designer on the hardware button decision (owner D, active)
  fact (absence): The user interface designer, Hannah (C), was absent because she was off sick and had sent her apologies.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer again proposed dropping the printer to save 250 euros. He withdrew the proposal after hearing that about a third of borrowers want printed slips.
  fact (plan_change): The book shelf height changes from about 90 cm to about 75 to 80 cm, and no controls will be above about 120 cm, to meet the wheelchair accessibility requirements.
  fact (plan_change): The RFID pricing task was reassigned from the industrial designer to the marketing expert, because library services already has a supplier price list.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer suggested supporting both barcode and RFID, as the user interface designer had proposed before. This was not decided because the cost is unknown.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F2_VAGUE_NO_OWNER [F2]: A task is mentioned vaguely ("someone should probably check the costs") and no one takes it. The gold action item has owner null and owner_unclear true.
  Required gold labels: action_items, edge_cases.
- F2_OFFERED_TAKEN_BY_OTHER [F2]: One person offers to do a task ("I could look into ..."), but a different person ends up taking it. The gold owner is the person who took it, and the history records the offer and the acceptance.
  Required gold labels: action_items, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.
